slides.title: Static and formal verification
slides.thesis: Every technique must discharge a named verification claim.
notes: Open with a decision the audience must make in this area. Ask which result they currently treat as sufficient evidence and keep that answer for the closing discussion.
The lesson selects a practical argument from the book. The study handout preserves the detailed examples, citations and worked artifacts.

slides.title: Learning outcomes
slides.thesis: Demonstrate these decisions on a real plan row.
bullets: Separate structural results from protocol obligations.
Qualify a proof by assumptions and abstraction.
Distinguish generated intent from independent checking.
Combine typed results through a verification plan.
notes: Read the outcomes as observable tasks. Ask learners to identify which one they can already demonstrate and which one currently depends on undocumented judgment.
At closure, require a concrete artifact or explanation for an outcome rather than a general expression of confidence.

slides.title: Route through the lesson
slides.thesis: Four blocks, each ending with a decision.
bullets: Establish the static boundary
Qualify the proof
Choose the application
Combine evidence without flattening it
notes: Allow eighteen minutes for each block: a concept, its engineering consequence, a worked interpretation and a short discussion. Keep the discussion tied to the evidence available in the example.
Reserve the final eleven minutes for the assigned exercise and application to the learners’ work. The timing is a course design allocation, not an engineering estimate.

slides.title: Static results have a subject
slides.thesis: Structural cleanliness does not establish functional correctness.
notes: Use lint to remove avoidable structural ambiguity before spending simulation or proof effort. Ask which failure classes the selected rules actually detect.
A clean report says nothing about a missing specified feature unless that feature has an independent check. Keep rule configurations and waivers attached to the result.

slides.title: Synchronizers do not define a protocol
slides.thesis: Independent bit crossings do not guarantee a coherent word.
bullets: Review the crossing structure.
Then review data stability, capture and handshake behavior.
notes: Draw a multibit value whose bits can be observed from different source updates. Individually synchronized bits do not make those updates atomic.
The structural CDC result and the protocol obligation need separate evidence. Ask what guarantees the data is stable during the destination’s capture window.

slides.title: Reset and unknowns need their own review
slides.thesis: A clock-domain inventory does not enumerate reset hazards.
bullets: Inspect reset assertion and release interactions.
Separate X optimism from X pessimism.
notes: Explain why reset interaction can cross boundaries even where clocks are shared. Do not infer RDC closure from a clean CDC report.
An unknown that disappears optimistically and one propagated pessimistically call for different diagnoses. The simulation configuration is part of the interpretation of the result.

slides.title: Discussion: a clean crossing report
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: A multibit status uses independent synchronizers.
The structural report is clean.
What coherent-transfer claim still needs evidence?
notes: Expected answer: the receiver must observe a value that corresponds to a permitted source transaction, not an arbitrary mixture of updates.
Ask for a protocol argument and its checker. Neither the absence of a structural warning nor the name of a synchronization cell supplies that argument.

slides.title: A proof verdict is a qualified statement
slides.thesis: Property, model and assumptions travel with the result.
notes: Have a learner say the complete claim aloud: which property, over which model, under which environment assumptions. A green result without these qualifiers cannot be transferred to a plan row.
Ask which legal behavior an assumption removes. A restriction introduced only to make convergence easier needs independent review before its proof can support sign-off.

slides.title: A bounded pass has a boundary
slides.thesis: State the depth and justify what lies within it.
bullets: A counterexample is a concrete failing trace.
A bounded pass needs a depth argument.
notes: Contrast finding a failure within a bound with establishing absence of failure beyond it. The latter does not follow automatically.
The chapter combines latency and scenario analysis, cover witnesses and prior counterexamples. Review completeness of the scenario enumeration as well as its arithmetic.

slides.title: Abstraction changes the trace set
slides.thesis: Know which conclusion survives the reduction.
bullets: Adding behavior can preserve proofs but introduce false failures.
Removing behavior can preserve failures but hide real ones.
notes: Use over-approximation and under-approximation explicitly. Explain why admitting extra traces makes a successful universal proof stronger while a failure may need validation against the concrete design.
Conversely, restricting traces can make a discovered failure useful without making a pass exhaustive. Record deleted behavior and the plan rows that cover it elsewhere.

slides.title: Discussion: assume away the failure
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: An ordering property proves after adding an assumption.
No owner can justify that environment restriction.
Can the row close?
notes: Expected answer: the result does not discharge the original unrestricted claim. Review or withdraw the assumption, then obtain evidence for the remaining legal behavior.
The chapter’s assumption register distinguishes proven premises, simulation checks and accepted arguments. An undocumented convergence aid belongs to none of those categories.

slides.title: Automation still needs reviewed intent
slides.thesis: Generated properties inherit their source description.
bullets: Connectivity and register checks scale repetitive obligations.
Review the description that generated the checks.
notes: A connectivity specification or register description lets the tool generate many mechanical checks. The engineer still decides whether that description captures the intended connection or side effect.
Generation can eliminate transcription drift while preserving a shared error in the source. Ask which review or independent evidence can expose that shared error.

slides.title: An inferred property is not an independent oracle
slides.thesis: Mining a design can reproduce its mistake.
bullets: Label the origin of generated properties.
Compare design-derived claims with external intent.
notes: Distinguish elaborating a reviewed specification from discovering patterns in the implementation. Both may produce useful properties, but they have different independence.
A property that faithfully describes current RTL can hold while the RTL violates its specification. Keep that distinction visible when admitting the property into a closure argument.

slides.title: Equivalence inherits the reference
slides.thesis: Preservation and correctness are different claims.
bullets: Define the correspondence and transformation boundary.
Choose sequential reasoning when state alignment changes.
notes: Use a combinational transformation and a retiming change to expose the difference between matched-state comparison and sequential equivalence.
A successful comparison supports preservation within the configured model. It cannot independently establish that the reference was correct, nor that excluded modes behave acceptably.

slides.title: Discussion: generated from one source
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: The register RTL and its checks share a description.
All generated checks pass.
Which error can both artifacts share?
notes: Expected answer: an incorrect or omitted behavior in the source description can be reproduced consistently in both artifacts.
Ask for the external specification review or independent check that would expose it. A second generated artifact is not automatically a second interpretation of intent.

slides.title: Allocate engines per claim
slides.thesis: A feature name alone does not select a method.
bullets: Match the oracle, state space and runtime need.
Keep each result attached to its plan row.
notes: Take one DMA feature and separate an invariant, a functional transfer and a long software scenario. They can need different engines and evidence boundaries.
The plan should explain why each engine answers the particular row. Do not choose a method merely because a tool or platform is available.

slides.title: Check the formal environment in simulation
slides.thesis: An assumption is a promise that another boundary must honor.
bullets: Turn relevant premises into simulation checks.
Cover important boundary behavior.
notes: The same expression can restrict a formal environment and monitor the actual integration environment. Explain why these are complementary uses with different verdicts.
A simulation check observes sampled executions; it does not prove the environment universally. Record that scope when discharging the formal assumption.

slides.title: Keep coverage evidence typed
slides.thesis: Simulation activity and formal coverage have different denominators.
bullets: Unify the plan, not unrelated percentages.
Handoff assumptions, exclusions and unresolved traces.
notes: Ask what an average of a functional bin percentage and a proof-core percentage would mean. There is no shared population to support that aggregate.
Use the plan row as the common unit. A handoff must retain the exact residual claim and its model restrictions so that the receiving engine does not unknowingly check a weaker problem.

slides.title: Discussion: the blended dashboard
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: A dashboard averages simulation and formal coverage.
The resulting percentage rises.
Which closure argument is still missing?
notes: Expected answer: the mapping from each typed result to the intended feature claim, with its own denominator and limitations.
Require the presenter to name what newly became established. A rising arithmetic aggregate cannot answer that question by itself.

slides.title: Exercise: coverage or mutation sensitivity?
slides.thesis: Choose an instrument for the actual question.
bullets: Proof-core coverage is offered as arbitration-change sensitivity.
Explain the gap and choose the appropriate instrument.
Include the chapter’s recommended proof-core scope.
notes: Assign book Exercise 14.4 in full. Review the four coverage kinds before the learner selects an instrument.

Expected answer: coverage measures aspects of exploration or the proof’s relation to implementation; none establishes that a property set detects a meaningful design mutation. Mutation analysis addresses that question. Explain the chapter’s selected proof-core scope and its cost and interpretation limits from the reading. Scope proof-core analysis to a handful of highest-value properties: it has the highest computational cost and its vendor-specific metrics are harder to interpret.

slides.title: What to change on Monday
slides.thesis: Make one existing verification decision reviewable.
bullets: Audit an assumption without a discharge owner.
Find a crossing with no protocol checker.
Replace one blended metric with per-claim evidence.
notes: Ask each learner to choose one of these actions in an existing project. Require a small, inspectable deliverable and identify the person who will review it.
Keep the change connected to the lesson’s evidence limits. A new dashboard, script or model is useful only if it strengthens the claim the plan row is meant to establish.

slides.title: Scope and next reading
slides.thesis: Use the handout for the detailed artifacts and sources.
bullets: Read the Static and formal verification handout and book Chapters 13–16.
Tool recipes and complete proof harnesses remain in the handout.
notes: Revisit the outcomes and ask the room to state a limitation of the strongest result discussed today. A complete answer identifies a model boundary, an assumption, a missing oracle or the scope of the underlying evidence.
Assign the detailed reading to the relevant chapters. The omitted topics are explicit scope boundaries, not claims that those topics are unimportant.
